shared_text:
The flight. A narrow-body airliner on a visual approach to an airport, in visual conditions.

The crew. The captain was the pilot flying and the first officer the pilot monitoring.

What happened. Approach control vectored the aircraft to the northwest of the airport, on a heading between a downwind and a base leg that pointed away from the airport. Roughly abeam the final approach fix, the crew reported the airport in sight and were cleared for a visual approach. They had planned to fly the visual approach backed up by the instrument landing system. The clearance came at an unusual angle to the final approach course, and the southerly wind made this worse. The captain disconnected the autopilot and hand-flew the approach, starting with a turn from base to final, while the crew slowed the aircraft and configured it for landing. At about 2,300 ft, the tower controller issued a low altitude alert on the tower frequency. The crew stopped the descent and checked, both outside and on the instruments, that the aircraft was at a safe altitude. Throughout, the crew kept the airport and the surrounding terrain and obstacles in sight.
safe_outcome: When the aircraft was back on the glideslope, the captain continued the approach. The aircraft was stable by 1,000 ft above the ground and landed. There was no conflict with other traffic. No one was hurt and the aircraft was not damaged.
bad_outcome: Another aircraft was crossing nearby. Both crews received TCAS resolution advisories and followed them, and the aircraft passed about 300 feet vertically and half a mile apart. A flight attendant on this aircraft was thrown against a galley cart during the manoeuvre and received a minor injury.
bracket_fill: [climbing / descending / crossing] = crossing; [this aircraft] = this aircraft
notes: Single narrative (first officer, pilot monitoring). Rule 3, removed: the reporter's view that night visual approaches are a terrain hazard; what the crew would do in future (ask for vectors to the ILS or a better intercept); and the view that a better vector would have avoided the event. Kept from that section, as a plain fact: the vector was between a downwind and a base and pointed away from the airport. 'Strange angle' rendered 'unusual angle'. Rule 5, moved to the safe ending: re-establishing on the glideslope, stable by 1,000 ft, the landing. Rule 6: airport, runway and the 080 heading removed. Judgement calls: day or night is left out because the coded local time (12:01-18:00) conflicts with the reporter's later remark about night visual approaches; 'visual conditions' is inferred from the visual approach clearance and the airport being in sight (flight conditions not coded). Bracket 'crossing': the aircraft stopped its descent at about 2,300 ft in the base-to-final turn and did not climb.
